intro.heading: What makes current flow?
lines: A battery gives a push. The push is called voltage, measured in volts.
The push makes charge move through the wire. That flow is called current, measured in amperes.
The wire opposes the flow. That opposition is called resistance, measured in ohms.
Ohm's law connects the three: current = voltage ÷ resistance. Double the push, double the flow.

what_changes.you_see: The current grows or shrinks with it
The line on the graph gets steeper, and the current drops

missions.instruction: Watch the meter. The battery switches on, the push spreads through the wire, and the current climbs to a steady value.
Drag the Voltage slider to 5 V or more. Watch the bright dot climb the straight line.
missions.hint: The V slider is on the right side of the simulation.

missions.instruction: Now push the voltage up by at least 3 more volts. The dot slides along the SAME straight line — that straight line is Ohm's law.
Raise the Resistance to 15 Ω or more. Watch the line get steeper — steeper means more resistance.
missions.hint: The R slider is on the right side of the simulation.

missions.instruction: Watch the two counting meters, one before the resistor and one after it. The counts stay equal. Nothing is used up.
This wire is a glowing filament bulb. Push the voltage to 10 V and watch the line bend — the hot filament does not follow the straight line.

key_ideas: Current rises in step with voltage, when resistance stays the same.
Current falls when resistance rises, when voltage stays the same.
Always check which quantity is held constant before you predict.

formula.reading: Voltage equals current times resistance. So current I = V ÷ R.

common_mistake.wrong: Current gets used up inside a resistor.
common_mistake.right: The same current flows in and out. The resistor drops voltage, not current.

ql_conservation.replay_prompt: Watch the two counting meters — the count going in and the count coming out stay equal the whole time.

ql_non_ohmic.replay_prompt: Push the voltage high and watch the bright trace bend away from the straight reference line.

elements.looks_like: a graph in the lower right, appearing from the second state onward
elements.means: the V–I graph. Current I is on the horizontal axis and voltage V on the vertical axis, so the steepness of the line is the resistance R. A straight line through the origin is Ohm's law; a line that curves upward means the resistance is rising.

elements.looks_like: two counting meters, one before and one after a marked band of the wire, shown in the conservation state only
elements.means: tallies of how many electrons cross each second. They stay equal, which is how you can see that current is not used up.

elements.looks_like: a faint straight reference line behind a brighter curving line, in the filament state only
elements.means: the straight line the wire would have followed if its resistance had stayed constant. The bright line peeling away from it is the hot filament.

welcome: Hi! I am Vidi, your guide for this lesson.
We will learn Ohm's law on a real moving simulation, one small step at a time. Ask me anything, any time, in the box below.

celebrations.m1: You saw it! The battery gave the push, and the current climbed to a steady value. That push is called voltage.
celebrations.m2: Nice work! You raised the voltage and the bright dot climbed the straight line. More push, more current.
celebrations.m3: Exactly! The dot stayed on the same straight line. That straight line through zero IS Ohm's law.
celebrations.m4: You did it! You raised the resistance and the line became steeper. A steeper line means more resistance.
celebrations.m5: Right! The count going in and the count coming out stayed equal the whole time. Current is never used up.
celebrations.m6: You found the limit! The hot filament bends the line — its resistance rises as it heats. The straight line only holds at constant temperature.

tutor.quiz_intro: Now let us check what you learned. 5 questions. Take your time — you have seen every answer with your own eyes.
tutor.summary_line: Great work today. Every step you took and every question you asked is saved, so you can pick up where you left off.
